articles.title: Car bomb tears through Colombian city wounding more than 20
articles.summary: The explosion is the latest in a string of attacks on buildings housing the security forces and government offices.
body: The explosion ripped through one of the city's central squares
A car bomb has exploded in the central Colombian city of Villavicencio, injuring at least 23 people.
The explosive device was detonated in front of the offices of the regional government, in the city centre, damaging several buildings.
No group has so far admitted carrying out the attack - the latest in a series using explosives to target official buildings and security forces' headquarters.

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella blamed "narcoterrorism", but gave no details. Armed criminal groups have recently stepped up attacks in what appears to be retaliation for an offensive ordered against them by De la Espriella.
Writing on social media, the president said that his government would "bluntly and forcefully" respond, external to "every drop of Colombian blood spilled".
"There will be no impunity and no retreat," he added.
It is the latest in a series of attacks targeting official buildings and security forces' headquarters
Three weeks ago, three adults and a baby were killed in a car bomb attack near army barracks in Tolima province.
And earlier on Monday, drones dropped explosives on the police headquarters in the northern city of Cúcuta.

The car bomb in Villavicencio went off on Monday evening - the eve of the 10th anniversary of the signing of a peace deal between the government and left-wing rebels of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc), Colombia's largest guerrilla group.
Following the signing of the deal, thousands of left-wing rebel fighters laid down their arms.
However, a significant number of Farc members, who did not agree with the deal, refused to disarm and joined dissident groups instead.

While forced displacement, child recruitment and the numbers of attacks on security forces dropped in the aftermath of the deal, there has been an upsurge in recent years driven by dissident Farc factions and criminal groups fighting for control of drug trafficking, illegal mining and extortion rackets.
Colombia's first left-wing president, who was in power from August 2022 to August 2026, tried to negotiate with these armed groups as part of what he called his "total peace" strategy.
However, the talks stalled and collapsed with several of the criminal groups violating ceasefires they had agreed to observe.
De la Espriella was elected on a promise to crack down on "narcoterrorism" and has been scathing about his predecessor's approach.
He has also been critical of the 2016 agreement, calling it a "false peace".

In a post on X, uploaded shortly before news of the car bomb in Villavicencio spread, he referred to the peace deal as a "mess", describing it as a "waste of public resources" and the "cause behind Colombia's ruin".

Former President Juan Manuel Santos and Rodrigo Londoño - the two men who signed the peace deal on behalf of the Colombian government and the Farc respectively - defended it in an interview with BBC Mundo ahead of the anniversary.
Santos said that De la Espriella was "totally wrong" to call it a "false peace".

"He wants to use, or has bought into that cynical and mistaken theory that the violence we see today is the result of the peace deal, when the exact opposite is the case," Santos said, arguing that the problem lies with the lack of implementation of the agreement.

articles.title: DR Congo says military aircraft missing as rebels claim to shoot down plane
articles.summary: A South African fighter pilot and a Ugandan officer are reportedly among those aboard the downed plane.
body: Congolese rebels said they had targeted a warplane preparing to bomb the town of Minembwe
The Democratic Republic of Congo military says it is searching for one of its aircraft, after rebels said they had shot down a warplane in the east.
The military said it had lost contact with a small Cessna 208 cargo plane on Sunday following "poor weather conditions". The fate of the plane and its crew remained uncertain, it added.
On the same day, the rebel Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) said it had shot down a warplane that was on a mission to bomb Minembwe in South Kivu province.
Four people were reportedly on board, including a Ugandan and a South African pilot, who is said to have been captured alive.
The BBC has not independently verified the rebels' claim.
It is also unclear whether the aircraft reported missing by the DR Congo military is the same one rebels say they shot down.
Uganda's military on Monday denied any involvement.
What's the fighting in DR Congo all about?
How former President Kabila became FRN rebel leader
A statement attributed to army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba posted on X said: "UPDF had nothing to do with the aircraft that was shot down in Minembwe. We have penalized that company."
The statement did not identify the company or explain what penalty had been imposed.
Gen Kainerugaba later posted that "no Ugandan is allowed to work for mercenary companies in [DR Congo]".
Uganda's denial followed the circulation of a video apparently showing a man being questioned beside the plane's wreckage.
In the footage, the man identifies himself as Ugandan and claims he had been sent by the government. The BBC has not independently verified the video or established the man's identity.
He and the alleged South African pilot are said to be the only other survivors.
South African media outlet Mail & Guardian quoted an FRN spokesperson identifying the pilot as a South African and a "mercenary [who] has no link to the place that he was hired to destroy".
"Unfortunately, we have a multi-country conflict in the eastern DRC," deputy FRN spokesperson Oscar Balinda told the outlet.
In 2022, DR Congo's army blamed M23 rebels, who are now part of the FRN, of shooting down a UN helicopter in which eight people died. The rebels denied it.
The Congolese government has in the past used foreign mercenaries to fight the rebels.
In recent days, fighting between the FRN and the government has intensified with the rebel group accusing the government of targeting heavily populated areas.
The rebels control large areas of eastern DR Congo, including the major city of Goma, after major territorial advances last year.
Aid agencies say the violence is increasingly disrupting healthcare services.
Over the weekend, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières said fighting in North Kivu had forced some of its teams to temporarily suspend outreach activities.
The fighting has also affected the response to the Ebola outbreak, with many health workers trapped, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The epicentre of the outbreak is in eastern DR Congo, which has been wracked by conflict for many decades, with some affected areas under rebel control.

articles.title: Russian governor detained in rare criminal case against regional leader
articles.summary: Andrei Chibis, head of Russia's northern Murmansk region, is the first governor to be detained for five years.
body: Andrei Chibis's wife rejects the allegations and he is expected to appear in court on Thursday
The governor of Russia's northern Murmansk region has been arrested on corruption charges in the first detention of a regional leader for five years.

Andrei Chibis, 47, is suspected of embezzlement and misappropriation of more than a billion roubles ($12.2.m; £9.3m) set aside to build an Arctic highway, as well as a further 39m roubles from the Murmansk construction budget.
Chibis is reported to have been detained as he arrived on a visit to Moscow on Monday and was taken in for questioning.
He denies wrongdoing but has made no public comment. His wife Yevgenia Chibis said "anyone who knows our family understands how ridiculous this is".
In a post on social media, she said her husband sincerely believed in the Murmansk region and thanked people for their words of support: "We really need them right now."
Chibis worked for several years as deputy minister for construction and housing, before becoming governor of Murmansk in 2019.
Murmansk is a key military point for Russia in the Arctic and is home to the Russian navy's Northern fleet.
The port of Murmansk is home to the Russian navy's Northern fleet

Chibis was re-elected two years ago after surviving a knife attack and is considered an active supporter of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Governors are seen as representing the Kremlin, and Vladimir Putin removed several in the months after the war began in February 2022.
However, until now no regional governor has been arrested since the start of the war, even though plenty of high-ranking officials have been detained in that time.

The Murmansk governor is one of a number of officials suspected of corruption by the Russian interior ministry's investigative department which, according to reports, alleged that a criminal group was set up in 2022 to embezzle money from the regional budget and move it abroad, including to Kyrgyzstan.
Another part of the case involves alleged fraud surrounding the rebuilding of a motorway between the two Arctic towns of Apatity and Kirovsk, which are 15km (9.3 miles) apart.
According to Russian news agency Interfax, a court will decide whether Chibis will remain in custody at a hearing on Wednesday.
He has been sanctioned by both the UK and EU, which accuses him of involvement in the illegal transportation of Ukrainian children to Russia and their adoption by Russian families.

articles.title: Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say
articles.summary: Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were reportedly given 74 lashes in Qom.
body: Parastoo Ahmadi's performance was livestreamed on her YouTube channel in December 2024
A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.
Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.
Ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.
This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.
In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.
At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said.

There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.
On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom.
"We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he said.
"The other lawyers and I even tried to get the enforcement of the sentence postponed, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately."
Pro-reform daily Etemad cited another defence lawyer, Mostafa Nili, as identifying the four men flogged alongside Ahmadi as Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia and Mohsen Lashkari.

"Parastoo Ahmadi's flogging for singing and dressing as she chooses is a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights and a chilling demonstration of the Iranian authorities' determination to suppress women's freedoms and to violently punish anyone who dares to challenge their discriminatory laws and policies," said Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).

Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.

In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".

Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.

Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.

In January this year, thousands of people were killed and tens of thousands were arrested when security forces crushed another wave of mass anti-establishment protests, this time sparked by the country's economic crisis.
Since the start of Iran's war with the US and Israel in late February, authorities have intensified their use of the death penalty against protesters.

According to the Norway-based group Iran Human Rights, at least 39 men convicted over January's protests and two convicted over the 2022 unrest have been executed, along with 16 people allegedly affiliated with banned opposition groups and 17 others convicted of espionage or collaborating with foreign states.
Another 121 protesters detained in January, including six women and five juvenile offenders, have been sentenced to death and are at imminent risk of execution, it says.

articles.title: Bangladesh's ex-PM Sheikh Hasina says she plans to return on 16 December
articles.summary: Hasina has spoken several times of her desire to return, but this is the first time she has set a date.
body: Sheikh Hasina has been living in exile in India since 2024
Bangladesh's former prime minister Sheikh Hasina has said she plans to return home on 16 December, more than two years after a popular uprising forced her from power.
Hasina, who has lived in exile in Delhi since August 2024, has asked the Bangladeshi government to fly her back to Dhaka, her spokesperson said.
The announcement comes amid renewed unrest in Bangladesh, where supporters of her Awami League party have staged protests despite a ban on its activities.

But it's unclear how Hasina will return. Last year, a Bangladeshi court sentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over a deadly crackdown on student-led protests that ended her 15-year rule. She denies the charges.
Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs Humayun Kabir dismissed the prospect of Hasina returning on her own terms.
"Sheikh Hasina will not be able to return to the country as an ordinary commercial passenger; she will be brought back in handcuffs," he told a press briefing on Tuesday.
Kabir also accused Hasina and Delhi of fomenting recent unrest in Bangladesh, alleging that they were backing "terrorist activities" in the country.

India's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a ​request for comment. In April, ​the ministry said it was ⁠examining Bangladesh's request to extradite her and that it wanted to "engage constructively with the new government and further strengthen bilateral ties".
Hasina fled to India on 5 August 2024 as tens of thousands of protesters descended on Dhaka, and crowds stormed her official residence.

What began as student protests against quotas in government jobs turned into a mass uprising against her government following a deadly crackdown on demonstrators. The UN estimates that up to 1,400 people were killed during the unrest.
On Tuesday, Hasina's spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali accused Bangladeshi authorities of forcing her into exile in violation of the country's constitution.

"Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on 5 August 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka," he said in a statement.

The choice of date is significant. Bangladesh celebrates Victory Day on 16 December, marking the end of its 1971 war of independence from Pakistan. Hasina's father, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, led the country's independence movement.

Abu Obaidha Arin, an aide to Hasina, described her decision as "deeply symbolic". "We firmly believe that she will celebrate this historic day among her people," he said, expressing confidence that she would once again lead Bangladesh.
Hasina's announcement - and Dhaka's sharp response to it - come at a time when the ousted leader is seeking to reassert her political relevance from exile.
The Awami League was banned from political activities in May last year under the interim government led by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Muhammad Yunus, which took charge after Hasina's ouster.

The party was subsequently barred from contesting February's general election, which brought its long-time rival, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), to power, with Tarique Rahman becoming prime minister.
But the ban has not put an end to street protests by Awami League supporters, who have also called for nationwide shutdowns demanding Hasina's return.
Hasina, meanwhile, has repeatedly spoken of her desire to return to Bangladesh, even as she has acknowledged the risks of doing so.

"I know that they may put me in jail or they may kill me, anything may happen, but still I have to go back," she told a gathering of journalists in Delhi over an audio link in August, on the second anniversary of her ouster.
Hasina's continued political activities from Indian soil have also complicated Delhi's efforts to rebuild ties with Dhaka.

India enjoyed close relations with Hasina during her 15 years in power and had hoped that the election of a new government in Bangladesh would offer an opportunity to reset ties, which deteriorated sharply after her ouster.
But nine months after taking office, Rahman is yet to visit India despite an invitation. He has travelled to China, Japan and Malaysia, and skipped the BRICS summit hosted by India in September.
Discussions over a possible visit in August coincided with anger in Dhaka over Hasina's remarks to journalists in Delhi.
The two countries have since resumed talks about a visit, but no dates have been announced.

articles.title: Comedian impersonates Trump's dance moves, mocks trade talks at Canada press dinner
articles.summary: The impersonator, Canadian comedian Mark Critch, poked fun at the US president's search for a new press secretary and US-Canada trade talks.
body: Watch: Carney and Trump impersonators take stage with real Mark Carney

Prime Minister Mark Carney brought a Donald Trump impersonator on stage at Ottawa's annual press gallery dinner, where he poked fun at strained US-Canada relations and on-again, off-again trade talks.
The impersonator, played by comedian Mark Critch of the sketch comedy show This Hour Has 22 Minutes, came out after Carney jokingly pressed an "emergency comedy button" during his speech.
Critch appeared alongside another actor impersonating Carney, played by Canadian sketch comedian Mark McKinney.
"We've got two Carneys here, it's a disaster," the Trump impersonator said after he walked on stage.

Using some of Trump's signature mannerisms, like his dance moves and his slightly hunched posture, he joked about the latest US midterm elections, which led to Trump's Republican Party losing control in Congress.
"I'm so popular we just had a big BLUE WAVE in the states," the impersonator said at the Saturday press gala.
He also took aim at ongoing US-Canada trade negotiations, saying,"We're going to have a great deal. There's only one thing standing in the way: me, because I'm crazy."
There were also jabs at Trump's search for a new White House press secretary following Katie Zacharia's exit, and at US ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra, who is unpopular among Canadians.
"I said 'find somebody who is less likeable than me,' and we got one," the Trump impersonator joked about Hoekstra.

Carney stood behind him occasionally laughing. The prime minister also delivered his own zingers, saying at one point: "This is a tough room. And I've been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator."

Both Critch and McKinney - the two impersonators - are fixtures of This Hour Has 22 Minutes, a long-standing Canadian sketch comedy show that has recently enjoyed viral internet fame for its timely skits mocking the Trump administration.
The skits, published directly on Tik Tok and YouTube, have depicted Zacharia's quick ouster, external and poked fun at rapper Nicki Minaj's, external support for Trump.
They have garnered millions of views, and even captured the attention of major US media., external

Critch and McKinney's appearance at Saturday's dinner is part of an evening of traditionally light-hearted humour, where Canadian politicians poke fun at one another at a gala hosted by the Canadian Parliamentary Press Gallery.
In a separate speech, Canada's governor general, Louise Arbour, joked about Carney's popularity and frequent global travel.

"Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he's supposed to be," Arbour said.

articles.title: King Charles and Elton John pay tribute to Australian music legend Molly Meldrum
articles.summary: The promoter and broadcaster helped define the music tastes of Australians for decades.
body: King Charles and Elton John have paid tribute to Australian music industry legend Molly Meldrum, who died aged 83 after a long illness.
Meldrum's family said he "passed away peacefully" at a hospital in Melbourne in the early hours of Monday morning.
The music promoter and broadcaster, born Ian Alexander Meldrum, helped define the nation's music tastes for decades, championing local artists like INXS and Kylie Minogue and global acts like Abba.
Known for his chaotic demeanour and trademark Stetson hat, he interviewed an array of stars, with the king on Monday calling him "a true giant of the music industry".

Born in Victoria in 1943, Meldrum displayed a love of music from an early age and went on to host the Australian Broadcasting Corporation's music television programme Countdown, and later a segment on variety show Hey Hey, It's Saturday.
Meldrum in 2014 became the first person who was not a recording artist to be inducted into the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria) Hall of Fame.
Meldrum lived with an acquired brain injury after falling from a ladder in 2011.
"Affectionately dubbed 'the Guru', Molly was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music," a statement from Meldrum's family said.
Among his most famous interviews was a 1977 sit-down with King Charles, in which Meldrum could not calm his jitters.
He stumbled over his lines, declaring: "Your Royal Highness... Oh, oh, I'm sweating like a pig".

King Charles reflected on the infamous interview for Countdown's 40th anniversary special, saying: "There is an old showbusiness saying which warns never to work with animals or children. But nobody prepared me for Molly Meldrum".
On Monday, an aide to the King said he had been "deeply saddened" to hear of Meldrum's death.

"His Majesty's interview with Molly is a moment he and many others will never forget - he hopes that interview will once again raise a few smiles as Australians honour Molly's legacy as a true giant of the music industry."
Elton John - a friend and regular interviewee - paid tribute to him as "an Australian legend and an institution", while pop star Kylie Minogue said she would be turning up the music in his honour.
"As a kid, I watched Molly Meldrum on Countdown every single weekend, in awe of the show and the magic it brought to our little TV in the lounge room."
"He championed so many Aussie artists and welcomed international artists to Australia in his own wonderful and inimitable way. I'm so grateful for his unwavering love and support."

Australia's Arts Minister Tony Burke said the country had lost an icon: "One of his greatest legacies will be the generations of Australians who grew up with his unmistakable enthusiasm and love of music."

articles.title: Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African police
articles.summary: South African communities tell the BBC of measures they're taking to keep women safe after a wave of horrific killings.
body: Okuhle's body was found dumped near a river in August. She had two children, aged three and nine, and was a civil engineering student
Tuku Nkosiyaphantsi found out his daughter had been killed from a post on Facebook.
It was August and he hadn't been able to reach 27-year-old Okuhle for days, although it wasn't unusual for her to drop out of contact from time to time.

Then one Saturday, two of Tuku's neighbours called him to say that they had seen that Okuhle had been reported missing by police on Facebook. They had also seen a photo of what appeared to be Okuhle injured.
"When I looked at this photo, I saw that the person in it was dead, and when I looked closer I realised it was Okuhle," says Tuku, 50.

After seeing the image, Tuku phoned a police officer he knew. The policeman confirmed the woman in the picture had been killed and her body dumped near a river in Kokstad, an agricultural hub in South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province, in the east of the country.
But because the morgue was closed for the weekend, it wasn't until Monday morning that Tuku was able to identify Okuhle's body.
When he did, Tuku saw she had been mutilated and her face badly beaten.
"It was very painful, so much that I cannot accept it."
Okuhle's father, Tuku, says he feels "ignored and unseen" by the government after his daughter's death
Okuhle had two children, aged nine and three, and was a civil engineering student.
She is among 581 women who were killed in the country between July and September, according to the South African Police Service.
Overall, there were 5,590 murders - 204 fewer than in the same period last year.
It is unclear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease on previous years as police had stopped releasing this breakdown until now.

There has been a renewed national outcry this year about the scale of violence against women after the partially naked and bruised bodies of 12 women were found dumped in public areas in Ekurhuleni, a district to the east of Johannesburg, this summer.
South Africa has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and femicide - the intentional killing of a woman or girl - in the world.
Am I Next? Fear and Survival in South Africa
The BBC World Service visits communities struggling to confront widespread violence against women

In response to this summer's killings, President Cyril Ramaphosa promised safety audits across every municipality to identify and address dangerous spaces for women, as well as an increased police presence in the worst-affected areas.
But in places like Kokstad, as well as Kempton Park, in Ekurhuleni, the BBC World Service saw people taking the protection of women into their own hands.
For Tuku, that means investigating his daughter's killing himself.
Months after she was killed, he says no-one has been arrested.
"It was just silent after we buried Okuhle - there was nothing at all. I so wish the police would stand up and investigate."

He believes police failed to review CCTV footage from a local government building in the town that may have shown who his daughter was with on the day she disappeared. The footage is wiped every seven days, he says.
The BBC approached the South African Police Service for comment but at the time of publication, no response had been received.

The police service has previously acknowledged shortcomings in its overall response to gender-based violence and femicide, adding that it was continuing to invest in addressing these challenges. Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia has said there needs to be "greater efforts" to prevent violence against women and children.
The killing of women this summer sparked widespread protests across South Africa
According to a 2024 report by the South African Medical Research Council, the number of unsolved cases of femicide was growing.
This year, Amnesty International said South Africa's police service was "under-resourced, poorly equipped, and insufficiently trained to respond effectively and sensitively to gender-based violence".
Tuku says he is now searching for CCTV footage and seeking out people who knew his daughter in the hope of finding leads.
Despite Ramaphosa's promises, he has little faith anything will change.
"I listened to Ramaphosa. The government acts only when something happened. We in Kokstad, we feel like we are ignored and unseen. The government does not care for us."

Asked earlier this month by the BBC what progress South Africa had made to keep women safe, Ramaphosa said the government would be allocating extra money in February's budget to deal with gender-based violence.

Speaking as he cast his vote in local elections, Ramaphosa added that the government had increased police numbers in the last three years "and we will continue to do so, so that there can be more visible policing".
Kokstad residents have started night-time patrols and are maintaining a curfew that advises children to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00
Okuhle is not the only woman to be killed this year in Kokstad.
Between January and October this year, the bodies of five women and three very young children were found in the town, with arrests only taking place in two of the cases.
In response, this summer, the community set up street patrols and a curfew for women and children.
Since June, children have been told to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00.

Kamvalethu Cetywayo, 34, from a local neighbourhood watch group, leads a group of around 15 men who patrol crime hotspots in the town at night, including areas where bodies have been found or trouble has been reported to them.
The patrols tend to take place between Thursday and Sunday because this is when people drink alcohol most heavily, says Kamvalethu.
Most of the patrollers carry sticks, whips and torches, but Kamvalethu has a licensed gun. He says the group will call police when they need back-up.
Asked how he feels about restricting the freedoms of women and children, Kamvalethu says the curfew helps keep them safe, is voluntary, and a temporary measure until police arrest the killers.
"With the resolution we made with the community, we get to assist them with this, but if people are refusing there's nothing we can do."
Even so, not all victims are attacked at night or on the streets.
Kgothatso says she was taking a taxi to work when the driver attempted to kidnap her
Kgothatso Mojela was kidnapped on her way to work in 2018 in Kempton Park.
She was in a taxi when the driver locked the doors and started driving in the wrong direction.
When Kgothatso told him he had missed the turn, she says he started punching and slapping her.
"Immediately, I just knew my life was in danger," says Kgothatso, who is now 35.

Kgothatso says she forced the passenger door open and threw herself out of the moving taxi, badly injuring her knee and causing nerve damage to her eyes. Two security guards, who were nearby, came to her aid.
She says her attacker was later jailed for a number of crimes, including what he did to her, but was released last year. Kgothatso says she now fears for her life.
Yet while Kgothatso was attacked by a stranger, according to the South African Medical Research Council, 60% of women murdered in the country between 2020-21 were killed by an intimate partner.
In the wake of her attack, Kgothatso has made changes to how she lives, including buying an imitation gun to scare off would-be attackers.
She has also stopped running alone, and insists on someone accompanying her if she goes to meet a client she hasn't met before at work.
Such precautions are all too familiar to many women in South Africa.
Zama says her running group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles
In September police urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone, "particularly in isolated areas" - after the killing of 38-year-old mother Elizabeth Moselakgomo.
She vanished on 9 September while out running. Her badly bruised, partially clothed body was found dumped near a busy motorway in Kempton Park three days later.

It was a killing that resonated deeply within South Africa's running community, including sisters Zonke and Zama Mthethwa. They started The Pack, a women's running group in Johannesburg nine years ago. Elizabeth would sometimes attend The Pack events.

articles.title: What strike on Russian ship in Libya says about spread of Ukraine war
articles.summary: Ukraine's sinking of a Russian battleship at a port in Libya raises the stakes of the war a notch, writes Frank Gardner.
body: Anchored in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.

The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi, co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?
The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch.
Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes, has called it "a dangerous escalation".
It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism.
Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga.

Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks – what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" – have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia.

The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.

And Ukraine has also been active further south in Africa where its forces have targeted Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps, the successor to the infamous Wagner Group that was accused of carrying out numerous human rights abuses.
It's not just Russia that will be alarmed by this latest Ukrainian operation in Benghazi harbour. The United Nations mission in Libya has already expressed its "deep concern".

Libyan officials point out that their country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war, although the Merkury and an accompanying cargo ship that was also hit were berthed in the eastern part of Libya controlled by the pro-Moscow warlord and self-styled "Field Marshal" Khalifa Haftar.
How Ukraine drone attacks on Russian ships unfolded

Throughout this year the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) has condemned all attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and today the global shipping community will be wondering whether this attack does indeed set a dangerous precedent.
If Ukraine can plan and execute such a bold attack on Russian ships in a nominally neutral harbour so far from home, where does this stop?
As the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches, this war has already been spreading, notably in other parts of Europe.
On Friday, several Russian projectiles landed well inside Poland's borders, just 60 miles from an Anglo-French exercise of forces intended to be deployed following an eventual ceasefire in Ukraine.
This, said Poland's PM Donald Tusk, was "a deliberate provocation" by Moscow.

It's not the first time Russian munitions have landed inside Poland, and therefore inside Nato territory, but observers have pointed out that Russia's probing of Nato's borders is becoming ever more brazen and some are calling for a firmer response.

But Russia is already heavily sanctioned by the West, with Europe having reduced much – but not all – of its energy imports from Russia, so the options for retaliation are limited, short of military confrontation, which no one wants.
Watch: CCTV shows explosion after Poland says airspace violated by Russian missile

Both Romania and Moldova have found themselves frequently struck by overflying Russian drones targeting Ukraine's Black Sea ports, while Bulgaria and Romania have suffered maritime drone attacks on commercial shipping just offshore in the Black Sea.
In the case of Romania, a Nato member, fast jets have had to be scrambled to intercept incoming Russian drones and there is a profound suspicion that these incursions are not all accidental.
The three Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – all have borders with Russia and all consider themselves right on the front lines in this war.
There have been a number of anonymous attacks on military industrial facilities in these countries, blamed on agents acting on Moscow's behalf.
Russia, for its part, suspects Estonia of being complicit in Ukrainian drone attacks on the Baltic involving overflights through Estonian airspace.
Hybrid warfare isn't new but it is on the rise.

It refers to the practice, by either side, of carrying out largely anonymous and unattributable operations using methods like cyber attacks, the burning down of warehouses supplying military equipment and the dispatching of drones, both for surveillance and loaded with explosives.
This autumn, Germany's Leipzig-Halle airport, which is used as a resupply hub by Ukraine's cargo aircraft, was targeted by three explosive drones that were discovered before anyone was hurt.
There have been other incidents involving explosive packages sent across Europe targeting Germany, Poland and the UK. Moscow denies any involvement.

articles.title: 'I want to destroy capitalism, not France': On the streets with the French ultra left
articles.summary: The BBC meets the far-left protesters French President Emmanuel Macron says are trying to bring down the Republic.
body: Watch: The BBC's Katya Adler speaks to protesters taking part in recent demonstrations

France is in turmoil. Crippling public debt, a "lame-duck" president with six months left in office, and massive social unrest - sparked by student protests which have erupted into looting and violence.

This Saturday marked the sixth weekend in a row of demos against soaring prices, worsening public services and alleged police brutality. Violence by protesters is down on last month but still present.
President Emmanuel Macron has publicly blamed riots on "delinquents" and "ultra-left groups" whose aim, he says, is to bring down the French Republic.
That's quite a claim – and one that needs examining.

The unrest in France has become a political football ahead of key presidential and parliamentary elections next year. The left in France blames the centre and right for the cost-of-living crisis that's making French people so upset and angry. They blame the hard left for fomenting violence (which they deny). While the nationalist right pledges, if elected, it will return order and security to France's streets.
So, who exactly are these "ultra-left" groups Macron speaks of? And how organised and dangerous are they?
It's infamously hard to speak to members of the radical left. They don't much like what they call mainstream media. We're viewed as part of an establishment many of them despise.

My best bet was to head out into the protests and try to approach people dressed in all black and ski masks or balaclavas (worn, they say, to hide their identity from police). It's a quasi-uniform associated with left-wing rioters or disruptors, known as the Black Block.
You see them at demos all over Europe. In France, they tend to appear from city side streets, as daytime protests are dying down, dusk is falling and riot police begin to emerge in full force.
The BBC's Katya Adler talking to a protester

French intelligence drastically underestimated the outpouring of anger, looting and destruction following protests last month. More than 1,000 police officers were reportedly injured, young protesters had bones broken and two reportedly lost a hand in altercations with police armed with stun grenades. Le Monde newspaper has an article, external it is constantly updating to investigate a rising number of reports of protester injuries. The French Insurers Federation estimates damages to shops and private property on 17 October alone - the day of the biggest riots - came to around €207m (£175.5m).
Since then, the French authorities are trying to tightly manage demos. Police presence is heavy. Protesters say heavy handed.

Towards the end of one of the protests this month, we saw would-be rioters vastly outnumbered, glass bottles and homemade paint bombs at the ready to throw at police. They were no match for the batons, stun grenades and tear gas the officers had to hand.
French police pepper spraying protesters during a demonstration by French high school and university students in Paris earlier this month

As we were being forcefully kettled in by police, I tried to talk to would-be rioters. Few wanted to engage but I then met 18-year-old Nas (not his real name) and friends. They would only speak to me if they could hide their identity. This was to avoid police detection, they said.
Milling, you could say provocatively, by baton-at-the-ready police – they seemed to fit a radical-left rioter stereotype.
"How can you justify the violence?" I ask them.
"Without violence, you don't achieve anything," one of them tells me. "It's the only way to get our voices heard."

"We come from an area with a bad reputation. Our schools are a mess. Our teachers quit. You need qualifications to get a decent job. There is supposed to be equality in France. We won't give up our fight."

These young men, we discover, come from the sprawling housing estates common on French city outskirts - the banlieues - associated with deprivation, unrest and second or third generation immigrant families.
They weren't politicised or organised by the radical left, they insisted. Just angry.
Left-wing rioters or disruptors, known as the Black Block, tend to dress in all black, wearing ski masks or balaclavas

Earlier, I had spotted two hard-left student activists, standing masked on top of a bus shelter, above the thronging crowd of protesters waving banners sporting the red anarchist sign and the symbol for the Antifa (anti-fascist) movement.
I put it to them that France has a proud tradition and respect for the right to protest but that the country has been horrified by the violence it's seen over the last weeks.
They were keen to downplay the rioting but - again – would only speak if they could remain anonymous.

"Violence ends up reflecting badly on our movements. We don't like it. But what's a smashed shop window compared to police using stun guns on protesting school kids? Also, people [in France] are regularly going cold and hungry. They're losing faith in this society."
How could they believe violence would bring about a juster society, I wondered?
They shrug off my question. In France, these days, the real violence is state violence, they say.
Some protesters don't support the Black Block's violence but say the state's violence is worse
French intelligence estimates there are 5,000 "ultra-left" activists in the country.

Anticapitalist Starflix (that's his codename) counts himself as one of them. The 17-year-old is also a member of the violent Black Block movement. We'd arranged to meet on the edge of the protest, by a narrow canal.
Fearful about being apprehended by police, he asked to remain anonymous.

He showed me a couple of homemade paint-bombs - eggshells filled with paint and sealed with medical tape that he throws at police officers. He carries them in his rucksack, wrapped in a royal blue Italia football shirt.
"We throw the paint bombs at the visors on riot police helmets, so they have to lift them up in order to see and that makes them suffer their own tear gas that they've sprayed at us," he tells me.
"We pick up stones and rocks too. Anything we find on the streets of Paris, to throw."

I put it to him that he and others in the Black Block are causing a lot of problems on French streets: damaging businesses, hurting police officers, destroying the demos for peaceful protesters. What is he trying to achieve?
As he's under 18, his parents give us permission to speak to him. They share his politics, Starflix tells me, but not all rioters - masked and dressed in black as he is - do.
"The Black Block isn't a single organisation. It's a technique. Some of us use violence to get government reform. I want to bring about a revolution.
"Other people are opportunists who use anonymity to steal things. When we all wear the same clothes, it makes it harder for police to identify us."
When I ask if he is scared he might get hurt or arrested, he admits he is but says what frightens him more is the thought that society might not change.
Social media plays a huge role in the riots. Starflix tells me he and his friends use Signal and Telegram to arrange to meet at protests.
"The Black Block isn't a single organisation," says protester Starflix

There are numerous websites and Instagram profiles, mainly hosted by left-wing organisations, offering tips for protesters and rioters, such as: keep your phone at home so police can't track you, cover your face to avoid being identified and emulate martial arts expert Bruce Lee and "be like water" - appearing and disappearing into crowds. That's advice passed on by the Hong Kong protesters eight years ago.

While not formally organising the protests or violence with these posts, could the fact groups host this information online be viewed as a kind of incitement or manipulation of youngsters whose feelings are running so high in France?
All the young rioters I spoke to insist they are not being herded or directed, but is there something bigger behind what's happening?
Ultra-left protesters spoke to the BBC on condition of anonymity

It takes our team a long time, but they manage to find a seasoned activist with the Black Block who would speak to us. I put to him Macron's assertion that the ultra left has organised groups that aim to bring down the French Republic. Is that true?

"It's totally false of the authorities to say we are all organised. And the intelligence services know it," the activist scoffs. "It's a manipulation of the French public to make them think there is an enemy within."

"Basically, people turn up to a protest, get dressed in black and do their own thing. The uniting factor is rage and not just in France. You see the same rage [in protests] in Italy, Germany, Spain. It's exploding by itself."

I ask if the anti-capitalist presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon and his France Unbowed party (LFI) are somehow linked to the violence. They are present at most protests, supporters handing out campaign pamphlets to the chanting crowds.

But the activist denies this, telling me Mélenchon is "a capitalist because he's part of the system". He says the LFI and the trade unions try to "calm" unrest, while he believes things need to be "stepped up a notch".
Why had he decided to talk to us, I ask - does he want to collapse the French government?

"I just want to say we don't love violence. I don't want to destroy France. We want to destroy a system that is a capitalist system, of course, but to change the society in a way that we think will be better for the most people, for more people.
"More and more find it hard to make ends meet. In the countryside, people can't even afford to fill their tank with petrol."
You have to leave the city, heading out into the gloriously autumnal French countryside, to meet some of the more organised, hardcore elements of the ultra left.
Limoges Town Hall, allegedly damaged by protesters, has become a symbol of the current state France appears to be in

This is a world of eco activism and known saboteurs. One man remains in police custody linked to the fire during protests at Limoges Town Hall last month. The devastated, yet somehow still elegant, 19th century building has become a symbol of the current state France appears to be in. An acrid smell still hangs in the air one month on.

The 34-year-old arson suspect, who insists he's innocent, comes from a hamlet near Limoges, known for its anarchist, environmentalist community. His father, a fellow activist, is also known to French intelligence. We approached the father and the suspect's lawyer for comment. They didn't want to speak.

Instead, we met a 39-year-old father of one, a local full-time ultra-left activist for more than two decades. Like the other individuals we spoke to for this investigation, he would only talk to us on condition he could remain anonymous.

articles.title: The rise and fall and rise again of Jensen Huang
articles.summary: Days after resigning while mired in scandal of extra-marital affairs, Nvidia's Jensen Huang is making a remarkable return.
body: It's being called a comeback for the ages.
For a long time it seemed that Jensen Huang, the leather jacket-clad founder of Nvidia, dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech", could do no wrong.
Then came allegations of two affairs - one with a businesswoman suspected of being a Chinese spy - that rocked the world of tech and the global stock market. Huang resigned.
Now, just 11 days later, he's been reinstated by the board, who says it believes he is the right person to lead the company.
So what do we know about the man who is once again at the head of Nvidia, a linchpin in the US's race for technology leadership with China?
Huang may not be a household name on the same level as Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg.

But his role in the tech industry, especially in relation to the explosion of artificial intelligence in the last three years, may prove more consequential. Nvidia dominates the market for the microchips that are used to power the new technology.
The company is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses.
Huang enjoyed access to the seats of political power on an unrivalled scale, being courted by both US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping.

His remarkable rise to the top of his profession saw him amass an estimated fortune of close to $200bn earlier this year, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, though that has since dropped to around $105bn.

Despite always donning his trademark all-black outfits and taking a playful approach to investor presentations, Huang has worked for years to present himself as a family man, someone who exemplified the American Dream.

Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to the west coast of the US when he was nine years old. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a Master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.
It was at college where he met his wife, Lori Mills. The pair were lab partners and married in 1985, eight years before Huang founded Nvidia.
They have two children, Madison and Spencer, who now both work in senior roles at Nvidia.

The company became a key provider of the computer chips and circuits used for gaming before it expanded in a new direction. It now creates the key processing chips used to power the growing AI technology.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after tech giant rocked by second affair allegation
Who could replace Jensen Huang as Nvidia's chief executive?

Huang has hailed AI as a "new industrial revolution" that is on a par with the advent of electricity. Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company and its customers include the biggest firms on the planet, Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic, all spending big on its products.

So it is no surprise that at a recent AI summit at the White House, Huang was picked out from a group of 42 to flank the president, alongside Elon Musk, both men with whom Trump has famously close relationships.

"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Jensen Huang, told the BBC, referring to the late boss of Apple. He added that Huang was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.
He described him as a "demanding" boss, who "really pushes his people to the limit".
But while Huang is "very brilliant" and a "world-class computer scientist", there's also "a level of arrogance" and "a level of self-deception as well", he said.
Huang had gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, he added, something that was "very important to him".

First reports emerged on 29 October in the New York Times that Huang had conducted a relationship with Alice Huang, no relation. US officials allege the businesswoman associated with Singapore-based firm Megaspeed is a Chinese intelligence asset.
Huang admitted to having been unfaithful to his wife and apologised for hurting their family.

But the reporting of a second affair, with Kimberly Powell, vice president of healthcare who has worked at Nvidia for 18 years, prompted a board meeting, followed by an announcement that Huang was stepping down.
He'd barely been gone, however, before a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign was launched, reportedly by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters.
The man himself said he would be "honoured" to return, should the board ask him.
Although initially showing no interest in reinstating him, the board has now done just that, saying his return was "in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".

articles.title: Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31
articles.summary: The COP31 summit in Antalya was the longest-running climate talks in UN history.
body: The COP31 summit in Turkey came as evidence of climate change could not have been clearer - 2026 brought glacier collapses, record European heat, and wildfires across Asia - but also when geopolitical divisions could not have been deeper.
The result was the longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on its central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts - to further climate action.
Despite two countries, Australia and Turkey, leading the charge in their joint hosting of the negotiations, they could not bring the nations together.

After a dramatic and fractious final day where countries walked out over the absence of mention of fossil fuels in the text and money issues, questions are being asked more loudly than ever before about whether the COP process can still deliver.
Here are five, key takeaways from the talks which the hosts hoped would become known as the "implementation COP".

This was the first COP since the UN warned that global temperatures are expected to exceed 1.5C degrees above pre-industrial levels. That is the threshold which countries agreed not to breach as part of the Paris Climate Agreement signed in 2015.
The draft agreement had acknowledged the uncomfortable reality that climate action to date has failed on its most crucial of targets.
Without agreement, that recognition has been lost.
Almost exactly a decade ago a group of the world's climate scientists - the official UN body the IPCC - warned what would happen if temperatures rose 1.5C vs 2C:
Sea level rise would be 10cm higher - that would expose 10 million more people to flooding, external
The ocean would become more acidic risking irreversible damage to some marine life
Extreme heat - that's hot days and nights - in every inhabited part of the world
In a 2C world extreme heat is expected to be experienced in every inhabitated area on Earth
Throughout the talks and during the final day, many countries still acknowledged that the target remained their north star of climate action.

"This COP sought to confront hard truths – that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with even more urgency to reduce emissions," said UK Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh at the close of the talks.
The draft had called for that overshoot to be kept as small and short-lived as possible – it also suggested something called carbon dioxide removal (CDR).
This is a process which takes greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere and has not been explicitly mentioned in a COP final agreement before.
Carbon dioxide can be removed naturally by planting trees - although there are limits to the scale and permanence of that.
There are other technological solutions, but these are controversial, external and are not well advanced.
This year's negotiations have exposed a troubling problem - consensus does not last forever.
On the central political agreement – the Antalya Pacts – countries could not bridge the divide on including language on fossil fuels.
And yet the very same pledge had been made just three years ago at COP28 in Dubai.
Rich nations also failed to put a figure to how much more money could be given to developing countries to adapt to climate change.
This is despite there already being a commitment from last year to triple the figure by 2035 from $40bn (£30bn) - but the interpretation of that pledge remains contested.
If governments cannot even agree to reaffirm commitments they've already made, it raises troubling questions about their ability to work together as the climate crisis intensifies.
Longest-ever UN climate talks end with no deal as deep divisions exposed

Minister Chris Bowen from Australia, who was co-leading the negotiations, pointed out at the end of the talks that the world is a very different place from when these commitments were struck just a few years ago.
"The situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory".
That was made apparent during the final meeting when pointed remarks were delivered. EU representative Darragh O'Brien said the talks had been "hijacked by some oil states".

Russian delegate Sergei Kononuchenko switched from Russian to English to directly address the EU delegation. He accused them of providing climate finance only in the form of loans to developing nations: "This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner".
It is a serious blow not just to climate action, but to multilateralism itself - the idea that countries can put aside their differences on other issues to tackle problems they can't solve alone.
Much of the coverage of COP31 has focused on the failure to get the central political agreement passed.
But much of the work at these summits is putting into action agreements made at previous meetings.

On money that is going towards adaptation for example, countries need to agree how is it being distributed, is it making an impact and how can this be tracked, and which areas are particularly vulnerable.
In fact, there were 164 other items on this year's agenda that were being thrashed out in the negotiating rooms.
And some of those were agreed at the talks.
The funds raised from a global system of carbon credits – money given in exchange for releasing greenhouse gases – will go towards helping developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change.
They agreed to advance a just transition framework designed to protect workers and communities as global economies shift toward clean energy.
But there were many more that could not be agreed and some will now be picked up at COP32, including crucially the work programme responsible for driving forward action on cutting emissions.
What governments agree in the COP negotiating rooms is only part of what determines the speed of the energy transition.
The International Energy Agency's latest World Energy Outlook, external points to another powerful force: energy security.

It says the disruption to oil and gas supplies through the Strait of Hormuz has been the biggest energy supply shock in history. The longer the uncertainty continues, the stronger the incentive for countries to switch from imported fossil fuels to electricity generated at home.
Renewable energy capacity is expected to grow 60% more over the next six-year period than the previous
The economics have been changing too.
Solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles have become increasingly competitive.
As clean energy develops its own commercial momentum, formal negotiations may become less important in determining its direction and pace.
Against the headwinds of inflation new investment announcements emerged at COP as part of the "Action Agenda".

This is the part of the COP process that tries to mobilise action outside of formal talks from businesses, investors and cities – this year the focus was on electrification. Turning more of our energy from fossil fuels to electricity.

"We are not entering the age of electricity, we have arrived at the age of electricity," Fatih Birol, head of the IEA, told the BBC. He says energy security and climate policies are now "closely aligned".
That doesn't make COP irrelevant.

Governments still have a crucial role in facilitating the transition, according to Dr Jennie Dodson, a senior director at the World Business Council for Sustainable Development which includes among its members the likes of Amazon and Apple.
"A key message from business is we can go so far, a lot of it is cost competitive, but there are policy barriers both around infrastructure and permitting".
Many are questioning whether the COP process is fit for purpose
COP31 has shown how the role of these annual UN climate conferences is changing.
For the first 30 COPs, the emphasis was on building the international framework for tackling global warming.
The great diplomatic breakthrough came in Paris in 2015, when almost every country agreed to keep global warming well below 2°C and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C.

Paris also established machinery designed to turn promises into progress. Every five years, governments assess collective progress in a global stocktake and submit new national climate plans, known as NDCs.

Then came further agreements: a fund for climate damage at COP27, a commitment to transition away from fossil fuels and triple renewable energy capacity at COP28, a new climate finance target at COP29 and increased support for adaptation at COP30.
The international architecture for tackling climate change has, in other words, largely been built.
Now comes the harder business of making it work. That's why this year's conference in Antalya, Turkey, had been billed as an "implementation COP".

articles.title: San Francisco is enjoying an AI boom, but worries about a crash are growing
articles.summary: AI employees in the industry's epicentre - San Francisco - worry that the sector is overheated.
body: The city of San Francisco is the heart of the AI sector
Lauren Goldboss is busy. The owner of a small San Francisco dog-walking company, she has been hiring staff and buying vans.
Fuelling the growth is her new office dog-walking service Paw Perk, popular with some local AI start-ups.
Her business is an example of how the AI boom in San Francisco is benefiting other sectors.
The city saw an exodus of residents during the pandemic and its downtown was weakened by remote work, but it's now enjoying a rejuvenation, with AI being the major driver.
Lauren Goldboss walks dogs for AI workers

Leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic – which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries – are based here. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, last week listed on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.
Thousands of other AI start-ups have also sprung up, external in San Francisco.
Signs of the boom are evident in soaring rents and house prices, falling office vacancies, and buses and billboards plastered with cryptic AI adverts.

But what if there is a significant downward correction in AI share prices and a resulting big fall in investment in the industry? The International Monetary Fund last month became the latest organization to warn, external that this was a possibility.

Concerns have since continued due to the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, the former boss of AI firm Nvidia, based south of San Francisco, causing some wider AI stock falls. However, Nvidia remains highly profitable, and Wednesday of this week it reported that its latest quarterly profits had doubled from a year earlier to $65bn (£49bn).
Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal
Wealthy AI workers send San Francisco house prices soaring
Follow the money: Who pays for the AI boom now?
What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco – no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles – be preparing for a possible crash?

One AI worker employed in the city is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come down… and I'm sure it will affect me," says the man who asked that we didn't use his name.
He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China.
But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?"
Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, says that a significant market correction is "totally possible".

Yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he says that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity.
"In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great."
If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south.
That's because the AI boom is very much centred on the city itself rather than the wider San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley.

One study, external found that 60% of all venture capital invested in US AI firms from 2023 to 2025 went to the companies located in San Francisco, dwarfing the significantly smaller percentage given to companies in Silicon Valley.
But some factors suggest that the impact of a crash in San Francisco may be softer than some fear.
For all the investment they have attracted, AI companies are employing relatively few workers in the city compared to previous tech booms. So there may not be that many jobs to lose in a downturn.

"Hiring isn't necessarily on the scale as we would have thought with the amount of venture capital and new company formation," says Jeff Bellisario, executive director of the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, a business-affiliated think tank.

Ted Egan, the chief economist for the City and County of San Francisco, adds that "because of AI, it is a good time for tech again in the city, but we are not seeing tonnes of overall tech job growth".
Despite the expansion of the AI sector, the city remains about 35,000 jobs shy of its pre-pandemic peak, estimates Enrico Moretti, an economics professor at the University of California, Berkeley.

Instead, much of the spending by AI firms in the US is going towards data centres and computing power, relatively little of which are located in the Bay Area. San Francisco might be the brains of the AI boom, but it isn't the brawn.

Nonetheless, a significant correction could still be "very painful" for San Francisco, warns Moretti. Less AI hiring and potential layoffs would ripple through the local service sector, likely to affect jobs in everything from restaurants, to retail, to personal services like dog walking.
"It is the spillover on service jobs that would actually be the main effect," he says.
Office vacancies could also rise, reducing downtown foot traffic, while rents and house prices could weaken.
Huge data centres are being built across the US to power AI

But AI isn't the only force driving San Francisco's recovery. Healthcare and tourism – which the city has been working to encourage, including by improving downtown safety and cleanliness – are also growing,, external which may help cushion against a possible AI downturn.
"Tourism is not fully back, but the growth has been healthy," says Egan, adding that it is a sign of confidence in San Francisco.
All told, Egan doesn't expect an AI crash to fundamentally alter San Francisco's economic trajectory.

"The city's economy has not been screaming during this AI boom, so I wouldn't expect it to grind to a halt if there was a slowdown in AI spending," he says. "I think of it primarily as a hiccup that we should expect, rather than a major course correction for the city's economy."

As to whether and how San Francisco's city government should prepare, there are limits to what it can do, note Bellisario and Moretti. But encouraging growth in sectors beyond technology and maintaining financial reserves could help.

For Goldboss, the dog-walking company owner, her philosophy is to "build while it is here". If the next tech bust comes – "always a reality in San Francisco" – she will try to adapt to what the market needs. "It is just the risk you kind of have to take," she says.
Office buildings emptied out but are filling up again - as homes
Wiped out by a hurricane, this US community is now a global energy giant
How the oil capital of the US welcomed a solar power boom

articles.title: Canada says it ‘does not report to the US’ after Pentagon memo criticizing military spending
articles.summary: US document criticizes the supposedly ‘atrophied’ defence capabilities of its northern neighbour
body: Canada is a “sovereign nation” that does not “report” to the United States, the country’s defense minister said after the Pentagon released a scathing memo that criticized the supposedly “atrophied” defence capabilities of its northern neighbour.

The document, released Tuesday, said Canada had “yet to make the hard decisions and tradeoffs” necessary to meet previous defence spending pledges and become a “credible partner in the defense of our shared continent”.

The Pentagon memo said it took Canada nearly two decades to finally reach spending promises made in 2006 “despite Canada’s role as a major G7 economy as well as one of the largest and wealthiest members of the NATO alliance”.

Historically, Nato members have fallen short of meeting the security organization’s funding goals. When Russia annexed Crimea in 2014, only three Nato members – the US, the UK and Greece – were meeting the alliance’s guideline of spending 2% of GDP on defence. By 2025, all 31 members with armed forces, including Canada, had reached the goal.

The document also suggested Canada faces significant operational hurdles in its air, land and sea operations, blaming political leaders for pursuing “parochial economic and commercial interests over military optimization”.

The Pentagon document said the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, was “laser focused” on modernizing Canada’s military, suggesting American taxpayers had been “footing the bill for its defense” for decades.
The defense minister, David McGuinty, told reporters he could not “divine” the thinking behind the Pentagon’s decision to criticise Canada’s defence spending now.

“The amount of co-operation we are pushing under NORAD [North American Aerospace Defense Command] has not changed. What we’re doing together at Nato has not changed. Our military-to-military co-operation has not changed. Our work on integrated air missile defence has not changed,” he said.
McGuinty also bristled at the suggestion from a reporter that the memo implied Canada required approval from the US when it came to its spending plans.
“Canada is a sovereign nation. I’ll be very direct. We don’t report to the United States,” he said.
The memo came as a Canadian official travelled to Europe to pitch a new defence bank championed by the prime minister, Mark Carney.

Isabelle Hudon, Canada’s lead negotiator for establishing the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank, is looking to cajole more countries into joining a global initiative that would lend to governments and contractors at low cost to support defense projects.

Ten countries have pledged their support but no others from the G7 have done so yet, with both the UK and Germany so far declining to join. Hudon says the €4bn in commitments secured so far is enough to start the bank up but she is aiming for up to €100bn.

Carney has made significantly increased spending commitments in defence. The country spent $63.4bn on national defence in 2025, meeting its Nato pledge to spend 2% of gross domestic product for the first time.
Last year, Nato members agreed to raise the goal to the equivalent of 5% of GDP by 2035.

Canada’s federal budget this month laid out a plan to spend about 4% of Canada’s GDP on defence and security annually by the end of the decade, and 5% by 2035, including the purchase of submarines and early warning aircraft.

Canada’s air power is a key point of friction with Washington. Carney’s government has yet to make a final decision on its order of F-35 fighter jets from the US firm Lockheed Martin and is weighing the possibility of purchasing Swedish-made Gripen aircraft instead. The multibillion-dollar purchase has been the subject of a political review for more than a year. The Pentagon memo warned that operating a “mixed fleet” of aircraft would “compound existing personnel shortfalls”.

articles.title: Hundreds of thousands could lose disability benefits under Timms plans for Pip shake-up
articles.summary: Minister’s review says Pip system no longer fit for purpose and recommends new test for who is allowed to claim
body: Hundreds of thousands of people face losing their disability benefits under plans being considered by ministers as part of a shake-up of the welfare system.

Officials are drawing up plans to redesign the personal independence payment (Pip) system for adults in England and Wales after the work and pensions minister, Stephen Timms, deemed it “no longer fit for purpose”.
Timms recommended a new test for who should be allowed to claim Pip, which would exclude those who do not incur additional costs as a result of their disability.
Related: What are the proposals for changing personal independence payment?

According to a study by the Resolution Foundation, this would apply to as many as one in six of the 4 million people who claim the benefit – though officials stress they have not yet decided whether any cuts would apply to existing claimants or just new ones.
Timms told MPs on Tuesday: “The system is no longer fit for purpose and requires a fundamental reset.”

He added: “Support should correspond more closely to genuine additional costs and needs. Cumulative and fluctuating impacts should be recognised properly, and the highest support should reflect the most severe needs.”
Speaking on Tuesday morning, Timms’ co-author Sharon Brennan made clear some people were likely to see their payments cut.

“It’s likely there will be a rebalancing process in which some people will get more related to their needs, and some people therefore might get less,” she said. “But it’s for the government to make decisions based on our report about eligibility and what that cost should look like.”

Timms’ report is the second half of the government’s attempt to slow the speed at which the bill for disability benefits is climbing, with Pip forecast to rise from about £16bn in 2019-20 to just over £41bn by the end of the decade.

Last week a report by the former minister Alan Milburn recommended scrapping Pip entirely for under-25s and replacing it – as well as part of universal credit – with more concerted help to get back into work.

Timms rejected Milburn’s approach, saying Pip was still an important system for over-25s who claimed it, but he opened the door for the government to make cuts through a new assessment to see who should be allowed to claim and how much they should get.

He made two recommendations that have been immediately accepted by the government: to make it quicker for people with severe conditions to be able to claim Pip, and to reduce reviews for those whose conditions are unlikely to improve.

For the remaining 90% of claimants, the review recommends assessments that would be tailored to people’s individual circumstances. This would be a change from the current system which awards payments in four bands from £30.30 to £194.60 a week.

It said: “Those with the highest additional costs, and so the most significant needs, should receive the most support.” But it added: “This benefit is not appropriate for those who do not incur any additional costs associated with being disabled.”

The Resolution Foundation survey found one in six people – about 666,000 – say they currently claim Pip despite incurring no extra costs as a result of their disability. Ending payments for those people would save the government up to £4.4bn if applied in 2029/30, the thinktank said.
Officials say no final decisions have been made about how the assessments will work, or whether they will apply to existing claimants or only new ones.
If they are applied retrospectively, government sources say there are likely to be transitional arrangements to help people move on to the new system.
Andy Burnham has said he wants to bring the welfare bill down “as soon as possible”, though he has rejected what he says is the Conservative approach of imposing “crude cuts”.

Officials involved in drawing up the government’s response say the key question is how quickly to try to generate savings from the new system. One senior minister said: “The aim is still to bring the welfare bill down, the only question is how quickly.”
Even with Burnham’s more cautious approach, however, the prime minister risks a row with his backbenchers over the recommendations from both Milburn and Timms.

Debbie Abrahams, the Labour chair of the work and pensions committee, told the Commons on Tuesday: “We need to have extra support for disabled people to cover their extra costs, and that applies to everyone of all ages.”
The Labour MP Apsana Begum warned about “the deep anxiety that disabled people will have about reviews recommending changes to eligibility without having specifics provided”.
Related: The Guardian view on disability benefits: Timms’s radical review is rooted in experience | Editorial
Campaigners and charities welcomed Timms’ review, which was drawn up in consultation with disabled people, but urged the government not to leave vulnerable people without a financial lifeline.
