Sarah Hughes, the chief executive of Mind, said: “It’s promising to see the recognition that Pip should be a cash benefit unless someone chooses other support in kind, that it is available to those in and out of work, and isn’t conditional on undertaking certain activities. However, in the wake of the Milburn review we know that many people – particularly those under 25 – are really worried that their lifeline will be cut.”

Svetlana Kotova, the director of campaigns and justice at Inclusion London, said: “It’s evident that when disabled people are actively involved in designing policy, the outputs better reflect the reality of our lives. Therefore, the government should prioritise the Timms recommendations over the reforms suggested by Milburn. The extra costs of disability do not start at 25.”
The Department for Work and Pensions said the new system would “help disabled people achieve better health, higher living standards and greater independence”.

articles.title: Israel attempts to jail Palestinian student at Hebrew University without trial
articles.summary: Mahdi Tounsi appeared to have suffered maltreatment at hearing where he was not allowed to hear prosecution case against him
body: Palestinian student Mahdi Tounsi appeared in a closed-door court hearing in Jerusalem, as academics and activists warned that Israel’s attempt to jail him without trial marked a serious escalation in attacks on Palestinian rights.
Yael Berda, a lawyer and sociology professor at Hebrew University, who has taught Tounsi for four years, came to court to call for his release.

“I have no doubt this is a case of political persecution based on identity and political activity,” she said outside the courtroom. “Mehdi’s arrest is part of a campaign that we’ve seen very much escalating since the elections.”
Her student was “almost unrecognisable” when he appeared on a video link in the courtroom, deprived of his glasses, with his hair and beard shaved and with visible bruising, she added.

Tounsi, a sociology and criminology student at Hebrew University in Jerusalem, was seized from his dorm on 8 November. He is held at Megiddo prison where documented abuse includes starvation rations, violent attacks on prisoners and rampant scabies and other diseases.

Thousands of Palestinians from the occupied West Bank are held under administrative detention orders but they have rarely been used against Palestinians who have Israeli citizenship or residence status in occupied East Jerusalem.
Prison authorities had not complied with a judge’s order to return Tounsi’s glasses, his brief public appearance on Tuesday showed.
Israeli prosecutors are seeking an administrative detention order, which allows for up to six months’ detention without trial or public presentation of evidence.
Security forces presented a summary of evidence in a hearing closed even to Tounsi and his lawyers, making a defence effectively impossible.

Tounsi’s arrest comes amid a racist campaign of delegitimisation against Palestinian citizens of Israel, whose votes were critical to stripping Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition of its majority in elections last month.

Noa Dagoni, executive director of Jerusalem-focused rights group Ir Amin, described Tounsi’s arrest as a dangerous escalation in political persecution of activists, particularly those “at the junction of human rights, dialogue and non-violent action”.

Many of the Ir Amin staff count Tounsi as a personal friend after years working together in his home community of Silwan, where Israeli authorities are forcing mass displacements of Palestinians, including to make way for a theme park.

Dagoni fears he may have been targeted for this work. “We’re very concerned that this [arrest] has to do with his being a non-violent peace activist, also dealing with the displacement in his community,” she said.
“The partnership of Israelis and Palestinians is very intimidating for this government because it can be effective, it can build real political power.”
Officers from the Shin Bet security force failed to appear in court to present evidence at a first hearing last week, so the judge reconvened on Tuesday.

Reflecting concern about the case, his family and lawyer were joined in the courthouse by prominent activists, Knesset member Ofer Cassif, diplomats from Ireland, the Netherlands and the EU, his tutor and the dean of students from Hebrew University.
Hundreds of Jewish and Palestinian demonstrators gathered in the street outside calling for his immediate release.
Many knew Tounsi personally from classes or activism, including Lana, a Palestinian citizen of Israel.

“Someone who I know being kidnapped was really frightening,” she said. “It makes me think of my place here also, how it might affect me and if there are more people who I know who are going to be arrested soon.”

Many protesters were angry with university authorities, including Arielle, 27, a former student at the same campus. “Israeli universities need to take accountability for this, like they can’t allow students to be kidnapped from their dorm rooms,” she said.

Hebrew University’s dean of students, Zohar Kampf, said the university asked to testify but its request was rejected. The university has not commented on Tounsi’s violent arrest, deprivation of glasses and other mistreatment.

Cassif, the Knesset member, called for a global pressure campaign. “Where is the international community, especially academia. What are they waiting for?” he said. “Speak up, do something, raise your voice.”

The police did not respond to questions about visible marks of abuse or details of the case against Tounsi. A spokesperson said: “The suspect was lawfully arrested as part of an investigation conducted by the Jerusalem District Central Investigations Unit concerning ties to an act of terrorism.”

articles.title: More than 300 Russians killed as Moscow props up Mali’s junta, leaked data reveals
articles.summary: Exclusive: Records list 349 deaths in three years in Mali and also shed light on Russia’s military activity elsewhere in Africa
body: When the attack on Kidal began before dawn on 25 April this year, the Russian fighters were caught off guard. Within the first hour, checkpoints on the outskirts of the remote desert city nestled among the rocky hills of northern Mali had fallen to the insurgents, who pushed towards the police station where fierce fighting erupted.

“Everything was happening at once. Explosions were going off all around us, people were shouting,” recalled a former member of Russia’s Africa Corps who was stationed in Mali at the time and spoke on condition of anonymity. “Nobody knew where the enemy was coming from.”
Related: Russia’s war dead: the hidden toll of the Ukraine conflict

The Kremlin-controlled forces and their Malian allies were facing a coordinated surprise assault by the al-Qaida-linked JNIM and the Tuareg-led Azawad Liberation Front (FLA), whose fighters used suicide car bombs and drones to break through the city’s defences.

Leaked Russian state records suggest the losses were heavy that day. Death certificates of Russian fighters killed in Mali, held by Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics agency, were obtained by the hacker groups Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow and analysed by the Guardian.

The records show that 43 Russians died in Mali on 25 April, including six in Kidal and one in nearby Aguelhok. Others were recorded as dying in the capital, Bamako, and in Gao, where rebels shot down a Russian military helicopter that day.

By the following morning, the Russians had abandoned Kidal, which Russian mercenaries had helped capture in November 2023 and which Moscow had since held up as a showcase of its growing influence in Africa.
In all, the records list 349 Russian deaths in Mali between September 2023 and September 2026, most of which the Guardian was able to link to known battles with rebel groups.
The figures offer a previously unseen glimpse into the human cost of Moscow’s efforts to prop up Mali’s military junta, in what has become Russia’s largest military deployment in Africa.
Two western officials who have travelled to Mali and were shown the data said the death toll was higher than previously estimated.
“That’s over 10% of Russia’s forces killed in action,” said one of the officials, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to comment publicly.
Related: Leaked data shows more than 1,000 Russian military suicides during Ukraine war
Moscow does not publish its losses in Africa, and its foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment.

The Wagner private military group, led by the warlord Yevgeny Prigozhin, first arrived in Mali in late 2021, a year after a military coup had toppled President Ibrahim Boubacar Keïta. French forces were ordered to leave the country as relations with the junta deteriorated, bringing an end to France’s decade-long counter-terrorism operation and leaving Russia as the regime’s main foreign protector.

Wagner handed over its operations in Mali to the Africa Corps in June 2025, two years after Prigozhin led a failed mutiny on Moscow that discredited the group in the eyes of the Kremlin. By that summer, British intelligence estimated that about 2,000 Africa Corps personnel were deployed in the country.

The Africa Corps, closely overseen by Russian military intelligence, currently provides backing to several African governments in return for payment or lucrative contracts granting access to natural resources.

Despite the Russian presence, Mali’s security situation has continued to deteriorate. In late July 2024, Russian and Malian forces fought Tuareg separatists for several days near Tinzaouaten, on the Algerian border.
Wagner at the time issued a rare statement admitting losses, including the death of a commander, but gave no figure. Estimates from Russian sources ranged from about 20 to more than 80 dead.

The Rosstat records list 70 Russians who died on 27 July 2024, all but one of them in the Kidal region. The figures make the battle of Tinzaouaten the deadliest single day for Russian forces in Africa since Wagner mercenaries first deployed to the continent in 2017.

The toll in Mali may have been driven up by Ukraine, which has extended its war against Russia to the Sahel. Kyiv has been assisting Tuareg rebels there, according to two people with knowledge of the operations. CNN has reported that about 15 Ukrainian specialists were deployed to Mali to help local rebel forces fighting Russian troops.

The records are probably an undercount. Registration often lags, and no Russian deaths in Mali are recorded for March 2026 although at least three Africa Corps fighters were reported killed in an ambush near Nampala that month.

The leaked data also sheds light on Russia’s military activity elsewhere in Africa. Central African Republic, where Wagner fighters guard the president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra, accounts for 30 deaths. While not all could be linked to known incidents, three men died on the night drones struck Wagner camps in Kaga-Bandoro in December 2023.

In Libya, where Russian forces back the eastern commander Khalifa Haftar and use his airbases as a supply route to their deployments in the Sahel, some of the recorded deaths were probably linked to a helicopter crash at the Maaten al-Sarra base in February 2026. On Sunday, Ukrainian drones sunk a Russian warship off the coast of Libya; it is unclear whether there were any casualties.

In Niger, where Russia’s Africa Corps moved in after the military junta expelled French and US troops, a Russian fighter died two days after Islamic State militants attacked Niamey airport in January, a previously unreported casualty.

Moscow has in recent months stepped up its effort to show it is back in control in Mali. On 6 October, Malian troops and the Africa Corps recaptured Kidal after what the army called an air and ground campaign.

A report this month by the US-based Conflict Insights Group (CIG) found that the Africa Corps had sharply increased its use of drones in Mali, including Lancet suicide drones, amid an intensifying air campaign.

The group wrote that the drone campaign had also targeted civilians, boostering support for the rebels. “Civilian deaths in the intensified air campaign, which the Africa Corps leads, are likely to aid insurgent recruitment,” it said.
A western diplomat who works in the region said the attacks in late April had punctured the image of Russian military invincibility that Moscow and the junta had cultivated among Malians.
“Russia still wields considerable influence in Mali, but patience with its military performance is wearing thin.”

articles.title: What are the proposals for changing personal independence payment?
articles.summary: Review by social security minister Stephen Timms is designed to ‘rehumanise’ system. What will happen next?
body: A government-commissioned review has urged an overhaul of personal independence payment (Pip), a key disability benefit claimed by about 4 million people, with the aim of making it more humane and effective. How will it work and who will be affected?

The government on Tuesday published the Timms review of personal independence payment (Pip), a non-means-tested cash benefit not linked to employment status that helps about 4 million people in England, Wales and Northern Ireland meet the extra costs of disability or long-term illness (Scotland has adult disability payments). The Timms review emerged from the wreckage of the Labour government’s attempts to cut £5bn from Pip in 2025, which was brought down by public outrage and a backbench rebellion. Pip support – between £30.30 and £194.60 a week depending on need – is highly valued by claimants – but the assessment process has long been widely seen as dehumanising, capricious, and crude.

The review, which began a year ago, was to find ways to ensure Pip was fair, effective and fit for the future while helping disabled people to “achieve better health, higher living standards and greater independence” including through work. Co-chaired by the welfare minister, Stephen Timms, and the disability advocates Sharon Brennan and Clenton Farquharson, it was “co-produced” in consultation with tens of thousands of disabled people through surveys and workshops. A key part of its aim was to find ways of rebuilding public trust in Pip and the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP). It was not asked to look at the overall cost of Pip.

It confirms Pip is not fit for purpose and calls for a reformed disability benefit founded on the principles of dignity, choice and control. This would help disabled people to participate in society rather than focusing on what they cannot do. It would remain a non-means-tested, non-taxable, primarily cash benefit to people both in and out of work. It would “more closely reflect” real life needs, and the additional costs of disability and would run on a twin-track basis: people with serious conditions, or receiving end-of-life care, would qualify for speedy awards and would not have to submit to repeated eligibility reviews; others would undergo an “impact assessment”, which would “review how a person’s condition affects their daily life” to determine whether they would get a cash award. Those who are eligible for an award will have the option to choose services instead of, or as well as, cash, similar to the Motability car hire scheme.

Although Timms was not asked to look at Pip spending, or how to reduce it, his report is acutely aware of anxiety in government over the rising Pip bill, which rose from £14bn in 2019 to £25bn last year, and is forecast to rise to £34bn by the end of the decade (although Pip costs have risen, the overall working-age benefit bill as a percentage of GDP has remained stable for over a decade). While not proposing cuts, the review emphasises that a new system must more accurately reflect the “real life” extra costs of claimants. This suggests some claimants would no longer be eligible for cash support, others would receive less cash than currently, while others, with higher needs, might get a more generous award.

Unlike the Alan Milburn review, which proposed that disability benefits including Pip are scrapped almost entirely for 18- to 24-year-olds, saving £3.6bn a year by 2036, the Timms review does not recommend different, age-related benefit systems for disabled adults of working age. Many disability campaigners were taken by surprise by the Milburn recommendations, regarding them as a crude attempt to make savings, and worry that many young people would be pushed into acute hardship as a result.

Charities have broadly welcomed the Timms review. It is seen as laying the groundwork for a new system that is potentially fairer and more compassionate than the existing one, particularly for people with complex, degenerative or fluctuating conditions. But there is also widespread nervousness that changes will leave some vulnerable people without support – about half of Pip recipients are in material deprivation, and most food bank users have a disability. There are questions about how people’s “real life” additional costs will be identified and calculated, and how cash payments would work alongside services. A red line for campaigners is likely to be a guarantee that changes do not deepen hardship.

The government is expected to formally respond to both the Timms and Milburn reviews in the coming weeks before a formal white paper setting out policy plans in the new year. Ministers are expected to push ahead with changes to Pip but face a major decision over whether to adopt the Milburn recommendations, which could put it on a collision course with charities and backbenchers.

articles.title: Gaza issues meningitis epidemic alert after steep rise in cases
articles.summary: Health ministry records 272 new infections in October, more than eight times the normal monthly rate
body: Gaza’s health ministry has issued an epidemic alert after a sharp rise in meningitis infections, with more than 270 new cases reported in October.
Dr Nidal Ghoneim, a senior official at the ministry, said the spread of the disease posed a threat to the lives of hundreds of thousands of people, including children.

Health organisations attribute the rise in infections to the destruction of infrastructure, overcrowded shelters and the contamination of drinking water with sewage – a crisis made worse by winter flooding and restrictions on humanitarian aid. Much of Gaza’s drinking water previously came from desalination plants and three Israeli-controlled pipelines, which were cut off at the start of the war and have only partially reopened.

Ghoneim told a news conference that 272 meningitis infections had been reported in the territory in October, more than eight times the normal monthly rate of 30 to 50 cases. Fifteen Palestinians have died of meningitis since the beginning of this year, he said.

“We hold the [Israeli] occupation fully and directly responsible for the epidemic outbreak due to its prevention of the entry of maintenance spare parts, sterilisation materials and fuel,” the health ministry said.

The UN’s humanitarian agency (Ocha) had previously reported 413 suspected cases of meningitis in Gaza between 27 September and 31 October, including 294 viral and 119 bacterial cases. About 68% were recorded in Gaza City.
Ocha said the increase in cases could be attributed to crowded tents and schools, the deterioration of shelter and sanitation conditions and exposure to unsafe water.
Related: ‘We ​are tired from all this suffering’: displaced families in Gaza brace for another winter of misery
Gaza’s water crisis is severe. Before the war, 80% of the territory’s supply came from an aquifer that is now contaminated by seawater and wastewater, making it unfit for human consumption.

For many, this means a stark choice between drinking an extra cup of water or saving it to wash their hands and prevent disease. Acute diarrhoea is among the leading causes of illness in the territory. About 15,000 cubic metres a day of untreated waste seeps into the groundwater from soak-away pits, particularly in the informal camps in al-Mawasi.
The World Health Organization said in September that microbial contamination in water samples had risen from less than 6% in January to nearly 20% in August.

In addition to disease outbreaks and shortages of drinking water and basic necessities, Palestinians continue to face attacks and ceasefire violations by the Israeli military, which has intensified its strikes in recent days.

Soldiers crossed into Hamas-controlled central Gaza last Wednesday in the first ground operation across the “yellow line” boundary since a fragile ceasefire was agreed in October last year, forcing dozens of displaced Palestinians to flee their tents.
Four people were killed and seven wounded in Gaza over the past 24 hours, according to the health ministry, bringing the death toll since the ceasefire took effect to 1,679.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and more than 176,000 wounded since the beginning of the war in October 2023, according to Gaza’s health authorities.

articles.title: Chinese police contacted members of WeChat group after they discussed Melbourne vigil for HungryPanda rider
articles.summary: Several members of chat set up after alleged murder of Feng Jianming say they or their parents were called by police from their home towns in China
body: Chinese police have contacted several people who were part of a WeChat group that discussed attending a Melbourne vigil for Feng Jianming, the HungryPanda food delivery rider allegedly murdered this month.

At least three members of the group set up after Feng’s death said they had been contacted, raising concerns that Chinese authorities may have been alerted to discussions about the protest activity either automatically or manually by the Chinese-owned messaging and social app.
Feng was allegedly stabbed to death near Queen Victoria market on the evening of Friday 6 November after he and another rider confronted a man who was allegedly tampering with their bikes.
Related: HungryPanda rider Feng Jianming ‘worked in the rain, delivering from morning until dark’ – until he was allegedly murdered

Angry members of the WeChat group set up in the immediate aftermath volunteered to host a vigil for the 49-year-old rider at the State Library of Victoria the next day, amid broader concerns about the treatment of riders by the company.

The group’s chat history, seen by Guardian Australia, shows that by Wednesday at least three members had told the group that they or their parents had been called by police officers from their home towns in China asking about their involvement with the vigil. The group, which by then had more than 400 members, was disbanded the next day after participants expressed fears about the police calls.
Members of the chat group declined to speak on the record, citing safety concerns.
HungryPanda, founded in the UK, targets the Chinese expatriate market in 10 countries. In Australia, it operates in nine cities, including Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Adelaide.

The Melbourne incident mirrored an event in February when HungryPanda riders in Sydney were contacted by police in China after a WeChat discussion about a proposed strike over wages on lunar new year’s eve.
More than half the WeChat group’s 155 members left and the strike was abandoned after the calls from police, which were first reported by the ABC.
Joy Wang, a former HungryPanda rider who was in the February group chat, said she had received four police calls from her home town in Henan province.
Wang said the police seemed unaware that the protest was in Sydney. When she explained this, she said they had threatened her with reprisals if she went back to China.
“They said, ‘You better not attend the protest, or we could go after you when you return to China,’” Wang said.

Jack*, who quit HungryPanda two years ago and now runs his own business in eastern China, said he had joined the February WeChat group to show support to his former colleagues. He had received three calls from police in his home town and was told not to take part in the strike.
Jack then quit the group chat. “I’m currently in China, there are things I need to consider,” he said.

Kitty Lu, the global spokesperson for HungryPanda, said the company had no responsibility for riders being contacted by Chinese police. The company was privately owned and independently operated, with funding from private and institutional investors in Europe and North America, she said.
Wang said the group members in Australia who were called by police had registered with WeChat under their Chinese mobile numbers.
She believed the use of keywords such as “strike” in the chat may have been the trigger for the messages to be transmitted to the Chinese authorities.

Jeffrey Knockel, a senior research fellow at the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab, agreed. He and his colleagues studied a 2016 wage protest in Jiangsu province and found that the phrase “industrial strike across the city” in the organisers’ group chat activated an automated mechanism on WeChat.

He suggested something similar may have happened in the Australian cases. Knockel also argued that WeChat may have flagged the group chat to a Chinese government organisation that would have then traced the riders’ details on China’s family registration system, known as hukou, and instructed local police to contact them.

WeChat has previously said that the data of foreign users is stored in Singapore, beyond the reach of Chinese authorities, but Knockel said if one member of a group registered their account with a Chinese number, the whole chat could be monitored by Chinese authorities.
Related: ‘Can you snatch it back?’ What happened after a HungryPanda delivery rider’s order was brazenly stolen in Melbourne’s CBD
WeChat did not respond to a request for comment.

Kevin Slaten, who leads the China Dissent Monitor at the US-based thinktank Freedom House, also thought the February calls might have been triggered by WeChat, given a rise in the number of labour disputes about wages in China during 2025 and early 2026.
“[The Chinese authorities may have] just assumed that these workers were in this wave of wage protests … not knowing initially that they weren’t physically located in China,” Slaten said.

But as the security apparatus was under direction to pay special attention to wage protests, the police may have persisted in warning riders to halt their action, even after learning they were overseas, he said.

The executive director of China Labor Watch, Qiang Li, has documented several cases of Chinese workers abroad being contacted by Chinese authorities after using WeChat to discuss industrial action. But these workers were usually working for projects controlled by China’s state companies.
Li said Chinese police had “overreacted” in the HungryPanda case but it was still alarming for Australia.

“Today we see these riders being called by Chinese police,” he said. “We could then see cases of anyone who uses WeChat, including Australian enforcement officials, their families, or anyone related to China, to be surveilled through this system.”

The home affairs department said it could not comment on operational matters but a spokesperson said it was “unacceptable for any foreign government to target members of our community to prevent individuals exercising their fundamental rights and freedoms in Australia”.
“Acts of harassment, assault, unwanted surveillance, intimidation, coercion or other threatening behaviour may constitute criminal offences.”
The opposition home affairs spokesperson, Jonathon Duniam, called on the government to do more to address the potential use of WeChat for surveillance.

“The Coalition has raised serious concerns about WeChat’s links to the Chinese Communist party, its censorship practices and its potential use for surveillance, yet the Albanese government has not done enough to address these risks or ensure proper transparency and accountability from the platform,” he said.

In 2023, a Senate inquiry into foreign interference recommended banning WeChat on government devices and establishing a national security technology office to monitor “high-risk” social media groups, including WeChat.
The government said only that it “noted” these recommendations.
The Chinese embassy in Canberra declined to comment on the HungryPanda allegations.

articles.title: Leftwing coalition leader calls for rental revolution as Spain heads for snap election
articles.summary: Exclusive: Ada Colau hopes public anger over housing will transfer into support for her Broad Front coalition in Sunday’s vote
body: The leader of Spain’s leftwing Broad Front coalition has called for a drastic rethink of the country’s entire housing rental system, and described the eviction of an 87-year-old woman – the spark for nationwide protests that in turn triggered Sunday’s snap general election – as “the last straw” for desperate tenants.
“We’re not interested in small changes,” Ada Colau, the former Barcelona mayor, told the Guardian in an interview. “We want to reform the entire rental sector.”

Public outrage over the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal from her Madrid apartment in September prompted the government, led by Pedro Sánchez’s Spanish Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE), to propose a series of changes to Spain’s housing laws. After the proposals were voted down by a combination of rightwing parties and Catalan nationalists, Sánchez called an election.

“When Maricarmen, an 87-year-old woman who had paid rent all her life, was evicted out of pure greed, that lit the fuse,” said Colau, who stepped out of the political limelight three years ago after failing to win a third term as Barcelona mayor.

The Broad Front alliance was founded in February to unite parties to the left of the PSOE, and named Colau as its candidate for prime minister on 12 October. “When I saw how many people were taking to the streets that’s when I agreed to be a candidate,” she said. “I thought, if I can be useful now, I have to be involved 100%.”

Polls have indicated that the conservative People’s party (PP) will win the most seats in Sunday’s election, but will fall short of a parliamentary majority, meaning the far-right Vox party could become kingmakers. A coalition deal between the PP and Vox would signal the return of the far right to government in Spain for the first time in the country’s post-dictatorship democratic history.

Colau’s alliance does not include the leftist group Podemos or the Catalan Republican Left (ERC) party. “I said to both Podemos and ERC we could change the front’s name, I offered to stand aside in favour of a consensus candidate, but the parties decided on a different strategy and I have to respect their decision,” Colau said.

Colau said she was sceptical of polls pointing to a PP-Vox majority. “I don’t think the majority of people want to go back to pre-democratic times,” she said. “People in the street don’t share this fatalism that the political right is going to win.

“People are very motivated, they’re very conscious that this isn’t an election like any other. This is the first time since the dictatorship that the far right might be in government and we might see the return of censorship, that we might see something like ICE in Spain, as well as attacks on groups such as the LGBT community and women.”

Polls suggest that a broad leftwing coalition encompassing the PSOE and all the smaller parties to the left of it won’t get enough votes to secure a parliamentary majority, but Colau is undeterred. She pointed out that at the general election in 2023 it was predicted that the right and far right would win, only for voters to return a progressive government, “admittedly with a very mixed and rather fragile parliamentary majority”.
She added: “At the moment we’re at about 8% and our goal is 10%. We believe people want to vote not just to keep out the far right, they want to vote for social progress.”

Colau has been a housing activist for over 20 years, and says there is little to choose between the PP and PSOE on the issue, blaming both for the mortgage bubble that led to mass evictions after the 2008 financial crash and then allowing the current rental crisis to unfold.

“We’re not interested in small changes,” she said. “We want to reform the entire rental sector in line with something similar to Germany and, above all, get rid of the vulture funds that are destroying our neighbourhoods and driving us out of our cities. Vulture funds contribute nothing, everything they do is harmful.”
Related: Will Spain’s snap election in November bring a far-right party into government?

She said that 13 funds controlled about 100,000 properties, and that the Broad Front’s support for a Socialist-led government would depend on it agreeing to expropriate these properties “at a fair but not a market price”.

She said that when she was mayor she managed to increase the social housing stock by assuming control of more than 1,600 homes that were in the hands of big property owners. “If we could do that in Barcelona with fewer powers than the government, obviously it can be done at state level,” she said, adding that the constitution stated that housing was not only a right but that it must have a social function. “As for regulating rents, it isn’t such a radical proposal, it’s something that’s practised in various European countries.”

As mayor, Colau won international plaudits for her efforts to prioritise people over cars, but at home she was equally loved and loathed. During her time in office she came under constant attack from the pro-car lobby and faced over a dozen “lawfare” cases, all of which were rejected by the courts. Much of the hostility directed towards her was misogynist. “I’ve always said I’d only return to politics if I think I can be particularly useful, if not, I’ll do something else, because there are many ways to be political, not just in institutions,” she said. “If I can make a contribution now, I will do whatever I can to stop fascism returning to this country.”

articles.title: ‘Menacing eyes’: Pope Francis’s diary details three encounters with the devil
articles.summary: Late pontiff’s innermost thoughts, reflections and fears are revealed in published passages from his private diary
body: Pope Francis wrote in his diary of encountering the devil and said he saw the “gates of hell” when he realised how serious a clerical sexual abuse scandal was, according to excerpts published on Tuesday.

The late Argentinian pontiff’s innermost thoughts, reflections and fears have been revealed in The Private Diary of Pope Francis, a book curated by his close aide cardinal Victor Manuel Fernández and being published globally in several languages.
The passages were taken from the black plastic diary that Francis, formerly Jorge Bergoglio, kept between 1992 and 2024.
In one of the most riveting passages, written in January 2021, Francis wrote that he had experienced “spiritual visions”, including of the devil.

“I clearly heard the voice of the devil,” he wrote, adding that he had seen him once “from the car” and again “in the choir loft” during mass about 15 years earlier when he was archbishop of Buenos Aires. Francis wrote in the published excerpts that he could not forget the devil’s “menacing eyes”.

He said he also felt the devil’s presence during his overseas trips as pontiff, including his visit to Chile in 2018, when he caused uproar by discrediting victims of the country’s clerical sexual abuse scandal during an in-flight press conference.

Francis apologised after his return to Rome, commissioned an investigation and said he realised that the victims were right and that he had been misled by the Chilean church’s hierarchy. He also called an unprecedented summit of cardinals at the Vatican in 2019 to address widespread clerical sexual abuse around the world.

“Devastated because of the situation in Chile and the dialogue with the journalists on the aeroplane,” he wrote after the trip. “I became aware of how serious the problem was … It was hard for me to admit what happened in Chile; I didn’t think it was so serious.”
A few months later in Rome, he wrote that he had a vision of the “entrance to hell” and “pagan seduction in full force” in the Chile scandal.
“I peeked in to look a little, and it terrified me,” the diary entry said. “I grabbed ⁠the rosary as a weapon. I thank the Lord for this help.”

The excerpts have been published after Fernández, the head of the Vatican’s dicastery for the doctrine of the faith, said he had been asked by Francis, who died in April 2025, to make his personal diary known to the world.

Upon Francis’s death, Fernández said he expressed concern to his successor, Pope Leo, that the book would be “left forgotten in some storage”, and he was permitted to publish passages, writing in the book that “the spiritual concerns present in his [Francis’s] heart are very clear and can do us good”.

The book does not contain the full diary and its excerpts are contextualised with comments by Fernández. Francis wrote his most confidential thoughts in an indecipherable code, according to Fernández, which is not included.

In another passage, Francis writes about suffering a two-year spiritual crisis, beginning in 2021 when he felt tempted by the devil and struggled to exert power over the Catholic church. The crisis came as his health deteriorated. He referred to fighting against not wanting to be someone who “used others like puppets”.
“It was all mixed with governance issues, pressure regarding decisions to make, and aridity and desolation,” he wrote in a December 2022 entry.

In his diary entries, Francis is also self-critical over his occasional feelings of “disdain, envy, pride”, and for having ignored a drunk man in the street who addressed him “because I wanted to walk in peace and quiet”.
“The arrogant, self-sufficient, cynical Jorge who lies to himself,” is how Francis described himself in an entry on 30 December 2022.
On 15 January 2017, he confessed that “for the past three or four days, I’ve been really angry and upset”.
In the book, Fernández also recounts Francis commenting on some senior officials, including the US cardinal Robert Prevost, who became Pope Leo in May 2025.
Francis called Prevost “a great pastor, a generous missionary, and an irreproachable man”, Fernández states.

Francis also offered kind thoughts about two of his most vocal critics – the Guinean cardinal Robert Sarah and cardinal Gerhard Müller of Germany. He said Sarah had “a refined spiritual sensitivity” and that Müller “seems aggressive, but he’s a good man”, according to Fernandez.
As for his own election as pope, Francis made one simple entry in July 2013, more than four months after he became pontiff. “They elected me pope on 13 March,” he wrote.

articles.title: Tuesday briefing: The fight over Pip – what happens when two reviews want different things?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: Stephen Timms’s review is expected to recommend a major overhaul of disability benefit assessments, days after Alan Milburn proposed a new system for under-25s
body: Good morning. Later today, the long-awaited review of the personal independence payments (Pip) system, carried out by social security minister Stephen Timms, will be published. It comes precisely a week after another review, by former Labour health minister Alan Milburn, proposed for Pip to be scrapped for adults under 25 as part of his shake-up of provisions for young people not in work. The suggestion blind-sided many of the disabled advocacy groups who contributed to Timms, but was a fillip for those on the right gunning for “generation snowflake”.

Whether you consider the unfolding Westminster drama to be the latest test of prime minister Andy Burnham’s leadership or an indication of whether you can pay for your transport to college next year says something about your personal circumstances, but also the current political climate, as we again find ourselves talking about disabled people’s lives in terms of how much they cost the state.

Why are Pip claims rising, what do disabled people’s organisations hope for from the Timms review and is it on an inevitable collision course with Milburn? I put these questions to our social policy editor, Patrick Butler. But first the headlines.

Russia | Figures from a cache of more than 11m death certificates, analysed in depth by the Guardian, give the most detailed picture yet of Russia’s losses in Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine

Tech | Jensen Huang made his return to Nvidia’s headquarters with a hero’s welcome on Monday after sensationally being reinstated as president and chief executive officer, less than two weeks after he resigned.

Brexit | Andy Burnham has said it would be “unthinkable” for the UK to rejoin the EU without holding another referendum, offering his strongest commitment yet to directly consulting the public if he concludes Britain should go back in.

Media | Channel 4 has suffered a blow after one of Britain’s biggest advertisers ditched almost all of its TV spending with the troubled broadcaster, in favour of a switch to online influencer marketing.
UK politics | Zack Polanski has given his backing to a paper that endorses Britain’s membership of Nato and the maintenance of the country’s nuclear weapons.

Perhaps you recall the images of disabled people protesting outside Westminster last summer, when campaigners risked their health in the sweltering heat to force Keir Starmer’s U-turn on proposed £5bn cuts to disability benefits.

Personal independence payments – brought in by the coalition government in 2013 – are made to people aged 16 to 66 to assist with the extra costs they face through ill health or disability. One of Starmer’s proposals to fix the “broken” benefits system by tightening eligibility criteria was met with a fierce backlash from campaigners, backbench MPs and the public.

Since then, Timms, who Burnham kept in post when he took over from Keir Starmer, has been tasked with reviewing the whole system and recommending reforms, as the government faces growing political and public pressure to reduce the benefits bill.

Before we get into that, let’s take a moment to consider the four million people in England and Wales who claim Pip. As Guardian columnist Frances Ryan pointed out, frenzied media speculation has a very real impact on vulnerable communities. “The priority is apparently to reassure Labour MPs and Middle England, as disabled claimants anxiously refresh the news page to learn their fate drip by drip,” she wrote.
***Why are more people claiming Pip?

To be clear: the UK spends practically the same amount on working-age benefits as a proportion of GDP today as it did a decade ago. But within that cohort, we are spending proportionately more on disability and health benefits, with large increases in Pip claims across all age groups and health conditions. (So that skywards graph on the front page of the Telegraph yesterday is factually accurate, yet inherently misleading.) Patrick Butler stresses that while there has been a sharp rise among younger adults, it is not just because of the myth that young people lack resilience, won’t answer phones and simply need to pull their socks up.

In truth, nobody is entirely sure what has driven this significant increase in disability benefit claims. One factor may be worsening population health post-pandemic, another may be the cost of living. “If people are really struggling, they will look around for ways to maximise their income,” Patrick says. Billions of pounds of benefits go unclaimed each year, so perhaps this marks a correction. What it’s not is an indication that people are “faking it”, he says. The test for Pip remains “incredibly hard”.
When did Pip become a culture war target?

After reading her column, I messaged Frances for a quick blether. She reminded me that “Pip’s origin story is a culture war.” It was pitched by the coalition government as a means of cutting the welfare bill, with Iain Duncan Smith assuring the rightwing media it would get people off lifetime benefits, which in practice forced those with, say, an amputation, to undergo pointless reassessments – presumably, Frances told me, to check their limb hasn’t grown back.

But the anti-benefits rhetoric has undoubtedly accelerated in recent years, with real-world consequences for people with disabilities – whether that’s repeated attacks on gen Z “snowflakes”, misinformation about fraudulent claims or harassment of blue badge users.

Last December, when I interviewed Tressa Burke, the powerhouse head of Glasgow Disability Alliance, she told me she was turning down an MBE in the new year honours list because of the way disabled people like her were being “demonised, dehumanised and scapegoated for political choices and policy failures by consecutive governments”.
What’s wrong with Pip, and how might Timms reform it?

Despite this, there is consensus across the political spectrum that Pip is in desperate need of radical reform. In an extensive consultation with more than 38,000 people and organisations, disabled people and their advocates pushed for a rethink of the current system of points-based assessments, which don’t account for individual experience or fluctuating conditions, as well as the return of indefinite awards for people with permanent conditions, which were phased out in 2013. (Research by the anti-poverty charity Z2K shows there were more than half a million reassessments last year of people with conditions such as cerebral palsy, learning disabilities and amputations.)

Setting out his plans for a “fundamental overhaul” of assessments in the Times on Monday, Timms said claimants with the most severe and well-evidenced conditions – about 10% of claimants – should undergo a fast-track process, while other claimants will face a new “impact” assessment, which examines their actual costs.

More broadly, his conclusions are expected to be very similar to a draft set of recommendations that emerged in September, which suggested some claimants could receive “in kind” awards, such as services, aid or training, alongside basic cash awards. In short, the recommendation is that any future reformed disability benefit should not be means-tested and should be available to all age-groups.
Is Timms on a collision course with Milburn?

First a word about comms strategy: compared with the Milburn review – where journalists were invited on government visits and given snapshots of particular ideas ahead of publication (pitch-rolling, as the lobby vernacular goes) – the energy given to promoting Timms has been markedly less.

Patrick was on tenterhooks yesterday morning waiting for the preview to drop (that woman from First Edition kept messaging him about it, which didn’t help) only to learn that the final report would be put before MPs on Tuesday with no further details released ahead of publication. “It’s hard not to come away with the impression that the government favours the Milburn findings,” he tells me.

And on one level that’s no surprise; Milburn projected £3.6bn in annual benefit savings over the next decade, a far more pleasing and less technical headline than Timms, who was examining how the benefit was administered.

But it sits oddly with how the Timms review has been framed by ministers – as a groundbreaking, “co-produced” policy initiative and a much-needed restoration of trust between government and disabled people after Starmer’s sledgehammer cuts.

Then, along came Alan. Last week’s Milburn review called for Pip to be scrapped for younger claimants, and for the health element of universal credit to be replaced by an additional cost allowance, part of a wider network of job-based help for this age group.
The shock among the organisations which had contributed to Timms was palpable, says Patrick. “The idea that you basically blow up Pip for younger people took a lot of groups by surprise.”

While no one is expecting Timms to be ditched, and many remain optimistic that useful principles will emerge from a process that has spent serious energy trying to understand and fix a system everyone agrees is no longer fit for purpose.

But the worry is that Milburn will take precedence when a white paper is produced in the new year. Disability campaigners were disappointed they were kept in the dark, says Patrick, and are likely to oppose any cuts to under-25s. “Why, they will ask, are the extra costs of disability any different just because you are young?”

An armchair made of brioche? A chandelier made entirely of sugar? I love it when art gets ridiculous. Chloe Mac Donnell’s look at the new generation of food artists is a delicious dive into a world where dinner is as much spectacle as sustenance. Shahesta Shaitly, newsletters team

Nine years after the Maltese journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia was killed by a car bomb, one of Malta’s wealthiest men was acquitted for involvement in her murder. Her son, a reporter for the Financial Times, writes powerfully (£) about his family’s fight for justice. Hettie

I’m fascinated by the obsessive creativity of fandom, and this brilliant exploration of fan fiction by Ekin Oklap looks at how an online labour of love became a million-pound publishing opportunity. Shahesta

I enjoyed Oliver Bullough’s long read about the battle to save a primary school at the heart of a Welsh village, and what he describes as the “slow-motion erosion of the foundations of life” in this sparsely populated part of Britain. Hettie

I have a soft spot for The Great British Bake Off’s glorious absurdity. As another series reaches its grand finale tonight, former contestants spill the beans on life inside the tent, including the area known as “fart corner”. Shahesta
Football | The announcement that the 2035 Women’s World Cup will be hosted in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland has finally come and it could have a massive societal impact.

Football | Gianni Infantino’s failed Fifa Forward Enterprise plan could have locked football in for up to 96 years while paying its management up to 5% of the scheme’s multibillion-pound value, according to documents seen by the Guardian.

Rugby union | The opening night of the inaugural Nations Championship finals weekend on Friday is poised to be played in front of around 40,000 empty seats, with the top tier of the Allianz Stadium in Twickenham to be closed.

“Huang returns to Nvidia hotseat as board bows to Trump pressure”, is the Guardian’s front page today, while the Times has “Trump chips in to secure return of Nvidia boss”, and the FT says “Huang reinstated as Nvidia chief”. Metro’s take is “Boomer Huang”.

The Mail has “PM opens door to second EU referendum”, the Telegraph, similarly, writes “Burnham opens door to second EU referendum”, and the Express says “You should be embarrassed by this bad EU deal”. The i Paper leads on “EasyJet, Ryanair and BA planes among 140 ‘jammed by Russian warship’ off UK coast”.
On the Ian Huntley murder trial the Sun writes “F*** it I’ll kill him” and the Mirror has “Hopefully I’ve killed him”.
Cop31 collapses: why did climate talks fall apart?

Countries at the Cop31 climate summit failed to reach a keystone agreement for the first time in 17 years. The talks, co-chaired by Turkey and Australia, were intended to produce a pact that would have injected urgency into climate action and financing for vulnerable states. Instead, the deal failed after a standoff over fossil fuels and support for countries exposed to the climate crisis. Guardian Australia’s climate and environment reporter Graham Readfearn tells Lucy Hough why there are calls for urgent reform of the Cop process.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

Most people avoid talking about death or dying, associating it with misery and pain. As Anna Gordon discovered in this moving picture essay for the Guardian, hospice workers, who help people at the end of their lives, are more focused on giving people in palliative care comfort, pleasure, and fulfilling their final wishes.

In September, education about bereavement and grief became part of the national curriculum in England, and a hospice in East Lancashire has been inviting primary schoolchildren to visit. “We’re not all wandering around crying,” one hospice educator in Hertfordshire told Gordon. “It’s not all miserable”.
